title: Mexico ex-prosecutor charged with treason over US drug raid
description: Federal prosecutors in Mexico have charged a former state prosecutor with treason for allowing US agents to join a raid on a suspected drugs lab in Ap
body: Federal prosecutors in Mexico have charged a former state prosecutor with treason for allowing US agents to join a raid on a suspected drugs lab in April without proper authorisation.César Jáuregui Moreno served as attorney general of the northern border state of Chihuahua from 2023 to this year.The involvement of Americans came to light after two US agents said to have worked for the CIA died in a car crash in Chihuahua along with two Mexican law enforcement officers.  Attorney General Ernestina Godoy Ramos said Jáuregui had allowed foreign agents to carry out activities reserved for Mexican authorities and had failed to share information. Jáuregui has denied the allegations.The former prosecutor, who is a member of the conservative opposition PAN party, was arrested at the weekend. A court hearing is scheduled for Saturday. A judge must still determine whether there is enough evidence to proceed with the case, Reuters news agency reports.Jáuregui also faces state-level charges in Chihuahua, including of abuse of public office. In a court hearing for those charges on Sunday, he denied that he instructed or consented to the involvement of US agents in the operation.Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has come under pressure from US President Donald Trump to crack down on drug trafficking but has repeatedly declined offers of US-led counter-narcotics operations in the country.She has been adamant that foreign officials can only operate on Mexican soil if given prior clearance by the federal government, and has insisted the Latin American nation's sovereignty should not be breached.The crash occurred on 19 April, when a convoy returning from an operation targeting suspected methamphetamine labs in a remote, mountainous area veered off the road and plunged into a ravine. Two members of the Chihuahua State Investigation Agency were killed along with the Americans, officials said.At the time, in his capacity as state attorney general, Jáuregui told a news conference that the Americans had been "instructor officers" from the US embassy engaged in "training work as part of the general and normal exchange we have with the US authorities".US media have reported that the two individuals worked for the CIA as part of an expanded effort to combat narcotics trafficking in the region.

schema.headline: Mexico ex-prosecutor charged with treason over US drug raid

title: Brian Stack: Family of prison officer killed by IRA receives state apology
description: Image source, HandoutImage caption, Brian Stack was shot in the back of the neck as he left a boxing match in 1983ByGabija GataveckaiteDublin correspo
body: Image source, HandoutImage caption, Brian Stack was shot in the back of the neck as he left a boxing match in 1983ByGabija GataveckaiteDublin correspondent, BBC News NI and Fiona MurrayBBC News NIThe family of a senior Irish prison officer murdered by the IRA has received a state apology on Wednesday for failings in investigations into his killing.Brian Stack, a father of three, was crossing a street in Dublin, after leaving a boxing match in 1983, when he was shot in the back of the neck.Stack, who was the chief prison officer at the high-security Portlaoise Prison, was left paralysed and died 18 months later, aged 49.There were three separate garda (Irish police) investigations into Stack's death, but no-one was brought to justice for his killing. The Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin offered an apology on behalf of the state during a sitting of the Dáil (Irish parliament).Stack's wife Sheila and her sons Austin, Kieran and Oliver were in the chamber for the apology.Martin said the Provisional IRA is "still in the possession of all the facts" on this case.'Address our concerns, Sinn Féin'The Stack brothers left the Dáil (lower house of Irish parliament) chamber when Sinn Féin TDs spoke during the State apology.Speaking outside Leinster House after the State apology, Austin Stack called on Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald to "address our concerns" around their father's murder."The IRA were responsible for the murder my father. The leader of the opposition has consistently said that the IRA campaign was justified," he said."The leader of the opposition did not dignify and respect my family by coming into the chamber today and because of that, we took the action that we did, in withdrawing from the chamber when Sinn Féin representatives were speaking."Image caption, The Stack family spoke outside Leinster House on Wednesday afternoon Speaking to reporters in Belfast, where she was being interviewed by the Police Service of Northern Ireland in relation to protests at Garvaghy Road, McDonald welcomed the State apology."I can only imagine the trauma that they have been through for a long time," she said."The IRA has acknowledged responsibility and expressed sorrow for the death of Brian Stack, has said that it shouldn't have happened and I think they made those statements very clearly more than a decade ago and I think that was the right and the correct thing to do."In a further statement, a Sinn Féin spokesperson said a number of senior party TDs made contributions in the Dáil, and that it was regrettable that McDonald was unable to attend due to her scheduled police interview."Our thoughts are with Sheila Stack and her sons. Brian Stack's killing was wrong and should never have happened. We are deeply sorry for their loss and suffering."Sinn Féin acknowledges the hurt caused by republican actions in the past. We welcome the Irish government's apology for the investigative failures that compounded the family's pain. They deserve truth and justice."Our position is clear: Investigating Brian Stack's killing is the responsibility of An Garda Síochána. We support that work and the family's right to answers."Apology means 'an awful lot'Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme Brian Stack's son, Austin Stack, said the apology "means an awful lot to us"."It's a great sense of comfort, to particularly my mother and to myself and my two brothers, because the state is officially owning up to the errors and the omissions that happened," he said.He went on to say that the serious crime review team looked into the first investigation and "they found 194 errors and omissions"."So I have, and my family have, met with several ministers for justice down through the years and we have a requested sight of that report. "And every time we've requested it, we've been told that it's an internally valid document and that we cannot see it."Austin Stack said that Wednesday would be a very emotional day for his family."My dad was doing a very difficult job at a very difficult time in our history," he said."He was awarded the Irish Prison Service's highest bravery award for that work that he was doing. And this is further vindication of him and his good name."Prior to the Dáil proceedings, the Stack family held a private meeting at government buildings with the taoiseach and Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan.'Utterly unacceptable'Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Taoiseach Micheál Martin formally apologised to the Stack familyIn 2007 the Garda Commissioner directed a review of the case by the Garda Serious Crime Review Team. Over 200 recommendations were made relating to the cases.This review led to "serious failings" being found as well as "the shortcomings in the management" of the earlier Garda investigation.These failures, listed by Martin in the Dáil, are: failure to keep a map made of the crime scene, a failure to keep a motorbike helmet found near the crime scene and linked to the crime, a failure to keep custody of material exhibits, including various fingerprints, samples and debris gathered during the investigation.The taoiseach also said there was a failure to document some potentially important aspects of the original investigation, including whether Brian's colleagues at Portlaoise Prison were interviewed and whether prisoners at the prison were interviewed.There was also a failure to interview the Stack family and to interview Brian's wider group of friends."It is plainly and utterly unacceptable that material that was potentially of evidential value to the investigation can no longer be located by An Garda Síochána."It is admitted by An Garda Síochána that these are serious matters that had an impact on the investigation," Martin said.He formally apologised to the Stack family for these failings.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, NI secretary Sir Chris Bryant was asked about the matter in the House of CommonsSpeaking in the Commons during Northern Ireland questions on Wednesday, Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said he "warmly welcomed" the apology.Asked about the matter by Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson, Sir Chris said Dublin doing so was "entirely right and proper" and went to the heart of discussions MPs had been having this week as they debated the UK government's Troubles legacy bill.He added that it was "incumbent on all of us to make fulsome and not mealy-mouthed apologies".'Regret'The IRA admitted killing Stack in 2013 after his family mounted a long campaign to secure the admission, and met Sinn Féin's Gerry Adams and a former IRA commander.Adams, at that time, expressed his "regret" to the Stack family over the killing.A Sinn Féin spokesperson said that "in a 2013 statement, a former IRA leader acknowledged that IRA volunteers were responsible for Brian Stack's killing". "The statement said the shooting had not been authorised by the IRA leadership, accepted IRA responsibility for his death, said it should not have happened and expressed sorrow for the pain and hurt suffered by the family."The spokesperson added: "As republicans, we acknowledge the hurt caused by republican actions. That suffering cannot be disowned. We are sorry for all the lives lost during the period of conflict on this island, without exception."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Irish foreign affairs minister Helen McEntee said the Provisional IRA "are responsible"Irish foreign affairs minister Helen McEntee also spoke during the State apology, she said: "The State failed you during their investigation into Brian's killing."She said Brian was "targeted" by the Provisional IRA and said "they are responsible"."To Sheila and to all of the Stack family, we are deeply sorry for all that you have endured, for the failures of the investigation and the additional suffering they have caused you, we are deeply sorry. I hope today's formal apology brings some measure of peace and comfort."Donegal Sinn Féin TD (member of Irish parliament) Pearse Doherty said the Stack's family "long search for answers deserves respect"."No apology can restore Brian Stack's life or return the years spent seeking answers but it can recognise the wrong done."He said the failures of the garda investigation "compounded" the suffering of the Stack family.In 2019, the family received an apology from then garda commissioner Drew Harris in relation to the handling of the investigation into the murder.In 2023, gardaí told the family that the file on the case - which was with the DPP (Director of Public Prosecutions) - was being sent back to police for further investigation.Stack was the only prisoner officer in the state killed by violence related to the Troubles in Northern Ireland.

schema.headline: Brian Stack: Family of prison officer killed by IRA receives state apology

title: Shakahola forest deaths: Paul Mackenzie's son says siblings were starved weeks before Kenya trial
description: Kenya cult leader's children still being starved weeks before trial, son saysImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Paul Mackenzie said educ
body: Kenya cult leader's children still being starved weeks before trial, son saysImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Paul Mackenzie said education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil"ByBasma El AttiReporting fromNairobiThe eldest son of Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie, convicted of murdering 191 people, says his younger siblings were still being forced to fast as recently as two weeks ago.Dan Mackenzie, 27, said he reported the case to police, who rescued eight children, including his five younger siblings from their grandmother's house, and took them to a rescue centre."They were basically forcibly fasted because they were denying food to them for almost three days," he tells BBC's Newsday.His father was found guilty on Monday of murdering 190 children and one adult who starved to death in Shakahola forest, near the Kenyan coast.He had ordered members of his doomsday cult to starve themselves and their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".Twenty-eight other cult leaders were also convicted of murder. Dan Mackenzie, who had initially defended his father, said at first he had struggled to understand the allegations against the cult leader, but came to realise the scale of the tragedy during the court proceedings."When I was 12, I was forced to fast for almost a week," he says. He also remembers church members beating him for hours to make him attend a service as a child. Now, he says he felt he had to report family members who still believe in the teachings in order to free his siblings. "I had to report my grandmother."The cult leader's doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil"."I left school when I was seven," says Dan.Now living in the coastal town of Malindi, Dan earns a living as a motorcycle taxi driver, supporting himself and his younger siblings.He said some people in the town had been angry with him because of his father's crimes, but others "had accepted him because he had distanced himself from that life"."I hope the verdict would bring some comfort to those who had lost friends and relatives," Dan tells BBC's Newsday.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, More than 400 bodies were dug up in Shakahola forestOn Monday, Stephen Mwiti, 48, who said he had lost all six of his children to the cult, welcomed the verdict."I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court.His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.Delivering her eight-hour judgment in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece".One of his co-accused told the court that Mackenzie had said anyone who resisted fasting must be forced to go to heaven "through kicks and blows".Burials in the forest where the cult was based were described as "weddings", with those who died celebrated as having "wedded with Jesus", the judge said.Mackenzie and other cult leaders also face separate cases involving terrorism, radicalisation and denying children an education.The murder verdict is the first ruling on the most serious charges against the pastor, who was arrested in 2023 after more than 400 bodies were discovered in shallow graves in Shakahola forest, near Kenya's coast.He is due to be sentenced on 6 November.Additional reporting by Thomas MukhwanaMore about the cult from the BBC:

schema.headline: Shakahola forest deaths: Paul Mackenzie's son says siblings were starved weeks before Kenya trial

title: Alberta's decision to stay in Canada gives Carney backing to take on Trump
description: "Vote like Canada depends on it," Prime Minister Mark Carney declared to cheering crowds in Calgary last week on a stage emblazoned with bright red an
body: "Vote like Canada depends on it," Prime Minister Mark Carney declared to cheering crowds in Calgary last week on a stage emblazoned with bright red and white "Forever Canadian" banners.It's a message that appears to have struck a chord with the electorate, as preliminary results show more than two-thirds of Alberta voters said they want to remain a part of Canada.But the future of the federation does still rest on its richest province.Alberta, with most of Canada's proven oil reserves and abundant gas and mineral wealth, is playing a pivotal role in Ottawa's drive to survive a punishing trade war with the US by diversifying trade, strengthening its economy, and forging new alliances on the other side of the world.Carney, the former central banker who grew up in Alberta, is now Canada's builder-in-chief – at home, and beyond its borders.Note the emphasis in his first statement after Monday's vote on separation in the province, as soon as the scale of the victory was clear: "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other."Albertans' overwhelming "yes" to stay in Canada gives him political bricks and mortar, too."Don't mess with Canada," warned Thomas Lukaszuk, a former lawmaker whose Forever Canadian campaign played a key role in this referendum's outcome.Addressing elated supporters in Edmonton, the provincial capital, as the "yes" count for Canada kept tumbling in, Lukaszuk underlined that this vote "will send a very strong message to the rest of the world".Everyone knows he's talking about the troublesome neighbour to the south – in particular its president, who keeps threatening to turn Canada into the 51st US state.The same day Albertans were voting on their future in Canada, Trump sent his own signal north at a rally in Kansas ahead of next month's US midterm polls."I will let you keep ice hockey, and I will let you keep your 'O Canada' national anthem," he promised before adding: "We're only kidding."For Canadians, it's no laughing matter.In the run up to this referendum, Carney reiterated a warning he's often sounded that "there are some outside our borders who are working to break us, so they own us" – even if he didn't spell out who "they" is.He didn't have to.And, in this defining time for the separatist camp, some in their ranks didn't hide their direction of travel. Some of their most prominent leaders admitted they travelled to Washington three times last year to meet US State Department officials and outline what an independent Alberta could offer – including a possible oil pipeline through the US to the Pacific.But the rest of the world may take only passing notice of what was, for Canada, an historic vote sparking conversations and concerns across the country, from coast to coast to coast."Short of a vote to separate, most foreign governments, with the exception of the United States, have little interest in domestic Canadian politics," says Professor Janice Stein, founding director of the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto."Foreign investors are focused on the time it will take to complete major infrastructure projects, a return on investment, and predictable regulations," she explains in a nod to Carney's long list of megaprojects he hopes will eventually turbocharge economic growth. They're all costly; many will take years to build.An ambitious blueprint already includes a proposed pipeline to the Pacific coast which opens opportunities for Alberta's oil to reach Asian markets – a move which also addresses Alberta's long-standing grievance that its economy has been stifled by federal policies, including environmental regulations.At a rally in Alberta last week, it was Carney's comment that the pipeline "will reduce our dependence on the United States" that triggered the loudest and longest applause of the night.After Monday's vote, Carney – the former UN Special Envoy for Climate Action and Finance –   pointed to "unleashing our full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta as its core". Political and economic pressures now seem to eclipse his green credentials."Build Canada Strong" has been Carney's mantra ever since he first entered politics, a complete neophyte, at the start of last year.At home there are possible wide-reaching repercussions from the final tallies in the referendum's nine other questions which dealt with issues ranging from greater provincial powers, the costs of immigration, and potential constitutional changes.Those results are certain to provoke debate, and deal making or breaking, involving Canada's nine other provinces and three territories. They all have their own grievances, too.The prime minister has had to defend himself when journalists ask if he is spending too much time on foreign trips with his charm offensive to build new political alliances and trade partnerships, including an unprecedented and still uncertain offer of associate membership of the European Union."I can do both and I need to do both," he recently replied with his signature bluntness before listing the more than 16 bills which went through Parliament in the last session dealing with everything from major tax changes, public safety, and the price of fuel.For now, Carney is riding high in the polls at home – including in Alberta, which doesn't traditionally support his Liberal party - in a long "political honeymoon" other beleaguered politicians would envy.And the plain-speaking politician's strong and steady response to Trump threats, including retaliatory tariffs, has seen his star rising on the world stage. It's an unexpected turn for a country which has often been missing from top tables and has sometimes even been dismissed as "boring".The Economist magazine decided to put Carney on their cover, on this week of weeks for Canada, with a perfect red maple leaf between his teeth."Mark Carney shows middle powers how to handle a dangerous world," reads one of its headlines, with an article which also focuses on Canada's "vulnerabilities" including Alberta's ballot."The broader takeaway from this vote might be that Canadian unity is in fine shape," remarks David Moscrop, political scientist and author of the forthcoming book On Nationalism."But what happens after Donald Trump is gone and Canada no longer has a single, bombastic target which drives Canadians to rally around the flag?" he asks.Carney's decision to recently walk away from trade talks with the US gave rise to another swell of Canadian pride and patriotism. But if this trade war drags on with a country which traditionally takes 70% of Canada's exports, Canadians will feel even greater pain in their daily lives.But today is a day to vigorously wave the maple leaf flag."It's a win for Team Canada and its resilience," commented CBC journalist Janyce McGregor during the public broadcaster's rolling coverage.

schema.headline: Alberta's decision to stay in Canada gives Carney backing to take on Trump

title: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)BySteve RosenbergRussia
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)BySteve RosenbergRussia EditorReporting fromMoscowAfter two days of diplomacy – in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg – is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard."In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace."I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said,  "but things are moving in that direction."All rather vague.It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Despite a "constructive" meeting between Witkoff and Zelensky in Oslo, Norway, the idea of a US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral summit does not seem to have taken holdIn recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky.That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader."Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says."Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?""Of course!"A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent.But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit.Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe."Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China."After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.

schema.headline: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace

title: The Gambia to pay Yahya Jammeh victims from the proceeds of the ex-president's seized US mansion
description: On Tuesday, the Gambia Reparations Commission said it was "pleased to inform victims, survivors and the public that it has received a total of $2,573,
body: On Tuesday, the Gambia Reparations Commission said it was "pleased to inform victims, survivors and the public that it has received a total of $2,573,414.10" from the sale of Jammeh's property.It said it was committed to ensuring the funds were managed responsibly and transparently, "with due regard to the rights and needs of victims and survivors".Jammeh lost to Adama Barrow in the election of 2016, first accepting defeat and then rejecting the results.He eventually stepped down in 2017 amid intense regional and international pressure.Troops from several West African nations, including Senegal, had been deployed to The Gambia, threatening to drive Jammeh out of office.In the end he agreed to step down and went into exile Equatorial Guinea.A national commission then discovered that the former president had 281 properties in The Gambia, as well as the one in the US and one in Morocco, and controlled more than 100 bank accounts.There was no way that he could have afforded this on his salary and it concluded that he had misappropriated more than $300m.Jammeh is accused of presiding over the murder of political opponents, disappearances, rape and torture.A commission of inquiry found that widespread abuses had resulted in the death of "240-250 Gambians and non-Gambians at the hands of the state or its agents".

schema.headline: The Gambia to pay Yahya Jammeh victims from the proceeds of the ex-president's seized US mansion

title: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to resume Ukraine peace talks
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Russia has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian citiesByJa
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Russia has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian citiesByJaroslav LukivUkraine's capital has come under a new missile attack, hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and the US president said the world was "the closest we've been" to ending the war.Several houses were hit on Wednesday night, injuring six people, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said.The attack came amid a new diplomatic push led by Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Witkoff met Russia's President Vladimir Putin in the city of St Petersburg on Wednesday - a day after meeting Ukraine's leader.Three-way talks were paused in February, after which Russia stepped up attacks as Ukraine ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.Speaking on Wednesday, Trump said: "The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we're getting closer to, by the way, maybe now the closest we've been."The US president has so far failed to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to an end despite his repeated comments that he would be able to achieve this.Trump's special envoy Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Tuesday. It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after the talks that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed. Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war. Russia blamed last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes during its general elections for their disruption.Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The latest talks between Putin (right) and Witkoff lasted about three hours in St PetersburgSpeaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict."Ushakov also told reporters that Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative".Ukraine and its European allies have disputed Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front.On Wednesday, Zelensky said he would accept a deal that would freeze the war along the current front line."We call it 'ceasefire' or 'stop killings' like President Trump called it. Freeze and stop. And of course this is minimum what we need from Russia today," he told Fox News, adding that security guarantees for Ukraine could be discussed after this.Figure caption, Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now"Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come."The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.  Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".He has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.He was also heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace".That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier.Zelensky - and Ukraine's European allies - criticised Trump's move.Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as "scandalous", and Zelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing "works now".Ukraine's military has also complained of speed restrictions to the US satellite internet network Starlink, which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia.US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisan group of US senators has called for an urgent investigation.Image source, Truth SocialImage caption, Hubbard had been in jail in Russia for allegedly fighting for UkraineBefore the Putin-Witkoff talks started, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American citizen who had been given a jail sentence of nearly seven years for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine.Trump said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary", while Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" for agreeing the release. When asked by a BBC reporter whether he agreed with such a description of the Kremlin leader, US Vice-President JD Vance said: "I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage. "Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said than about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family."

schema.headline: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to resume Ukraine peace talks

title: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
description: Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 300 people, including dozens travelling to a fu
body: Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 300 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral.The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 153 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said.A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF.The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011.South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador to lodge a formal protest. There are fears the conflict could spill across the border.The attack in Abyei, which borders West Kordofan, took place on Monday around 11:30 local time (09:30 GMT) targeting Amiet Market around 10km (six miles) from Abyei town, the region's Information Minister Yohana Akol Ngor told Radio Tamazuj, which broadcasts from the Netherlands to audiences on the Sudan-South Sudan border.On Tuesday, the minister confirmed to the Associated Press and Reuters that the death toll had risen from 73 to 153 people."It is a horrible and shocking situation," AP quotes him as saying.BBC Verify has studied satellite images that show extensive burnt buildings in the north-east corner of Amiet Market, which is also known in Arabic as Al-Na'am Market. Older images from the area show it is usually full of trucks.It has also verified footage filmed near the market that shows a large plume of smoke, at least one petrol tanker and someone talking about five missiles being fired. Another verified video shows two massive, separate fires coming from buildings near that section of the market."The market was completely destroyed. The bombing spread terror and fear among the local population," market trader Fadlallah Adam Hamouda told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily.Another trader told the BBC the attack had come as shock as UN peacekeepers have been in Abyei since 2011 - with more than 2,800 uniformed personnel currently deployed."Our area is a weapons-free zone under United Nations protection, yet it was targeted by drones," he said."The attack caused extensive material damage after the fuel market was struck, sparking a massive fire that spread to nearby homes."Earlier, Ngor told Reuters that emergency workers had struggled to retrieve the bodies because of fires caused by the strikes.On Monday, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said it had also received people wounded in the attack at Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town."So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted. We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," MSF's Christian Lindauer, the charity's manager at the hospital, said in a statement.Meanwhile, a drone strike near the airport in Khartoum on Monday has killed four people, including three children, the AFP news agency reports, quoting a medical source.It also cited a military source as saying air defences in the Sudanese capital had downed several other drones launched by the RSF towards the airport.Fighting in Kordofan, a strategic area rich in gold and oil, has intensified over the last year after the army regained control of Khartoum from the RSF.

schema.headline: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say

title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
description: Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with the largest ever fine against it for its business practices.A judge in New
body: Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with the largest ever fine against it for its business practices.A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data."The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices".Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful.The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety.New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal.That firm utilised data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too. Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added.Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been.They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times."For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday. "Today's result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable."The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional. Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter.He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years", stretching from 2010 to 2021. Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public", Judge Mathew wrote in his order.While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine.It follows a $5bn fine levied by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 against the company over its data privacy practices.New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this year also fined Meta almost $1bn for misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children.The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children".As large as the fines against Meta are, the company is spending much more on infrastructure as it works to catch up with other tech companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) race.Zuckerberg said during a call with financial analysts that Meta's consumer-focused AI tool Muse was already being used by 10 million people. "Growing Muse to serve billions of people is both our mission and our strategy," Zuckerberg said.  To that end, Meta expects to spend at least $135bn this year on mostly AI projects, but could spend up to $145bn.The company is spending so much on AI that it reported negative cash flow of more than $2bn - an apparent first for Meta since it listed on the public stock market 14 years ago, according to a BBC review of its past financial documents.Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments. So, Meta is now spending more than it brings in, even as it brings in more money than ever.Meta's revenue increased 26% for July to September compared to a year ago, hitting $64.5bn. Its profits also tripled to $9.8bn.Still, the company intends to spend more on AI investments. Meta's chief financial officer Susan Li announced a new stock split on the call, in which existing Meta shareholders will receive one new share on non-voting stock. Li said the new class of stock was not yet intended for one specific investment, but she alluded to ongoing costs related to AI and said the company could use "more funding flexibility" next year.

schema.headline: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy

title: Kim Jong Un: Why do rumours about his death keep coming back?
description: Kim Jong Un has appeared in North Korean state media looking remarkably healthy for a man rumoured to have died from a brain haemorrhage.Photographs p
body: Kim Jong Un has appeared in North Korean state media looking remarkably healthy for a man rumoured to have died from a brain haemorrhage.Photographs published by state newspaper Rodong Sinmun show the 42-year-old dictator touring what the paper said was a clothing and footwear exhibition with his daughter.The images emerged hours after a Chinese dissident who lives in the US claimed, without evidence, that Kim had been taken to a hospital in Beijing in a coma and had died.For those who watch North Korea closely, this kind of rumour has become almost routine.In one of the world's most secretive states, facts are often difficult to verify, creating fertile ground for speculation.This latest claim originated with Wanjun Xie, who identifies himself as chairman of the Chinese Democratic Party, a group banned by Chinese authorities. He has previously circulated unverified claims, including speculation about the death of Chinese leader Xi Jinping.Xie alleged that Kim suffered a severe brain haemorrhage and was transferred to Beijing because North Korea lacked the medical facilities to treat him. He claimed Kim later died and that his body had been secretly returned to North Korea, with the regime concealing his death.Yet the photographs tell a different story. Kim is seen examining displays, accompanied by Kim Ju Ae and his usual entourage of officials. While there is no way to know exactly when the images were taken, there are other reasons to doubt the claim.There would probably be signs beyond North Korea's borders if there were a sudden collapse in Kim's health.China could tighten security along its frontier to prepare for potential instability or refugee flows. Activity around North Korean diplomatic missions might also increase. Defectors in South Korea often receive information through informal networks along the Chinese border. None of this has happened. South Korean intelligence officials, meanwhile, told Yonhap they had heard nothing to support the reports.The rumour also echoes previous false alarms.In 2020, a high-profile North Korean defector claimed he was "99% certain" Kim had died following cardiovascular surgery. Not long afterwards, Kim appeared in public and the claim unravelled.So why do these rumours keep resurfacing? The first reason is succession.North Korea has been ruled by the Kim family for three generations, but what happens after Kim Jong Un remains less certain than it was for his predecessors.Kim Il Sung spent decades preparing his son, Kim Jong Il, for power. By the time Kim Il Sung died in 1994, the succession plan was firmly established. Kim Jong Il's transition was relatively smooth.Kim Jong Un's rise was faster and more precarious. After Kim Jong Il suffered a stroke in 2008, his youngest son was rapidly promoted through the ranks. By the time his father died in 2011, he had been publicly identified as the future leader. Even so, Kim Jong Un spent years consolidating power, purging rivals and eliminating perceived threats.Today, South Korea's intelligence agency believes he may be preparing his daughter as a successor. She has increasingly appeared at high-profile events and military displays.But she is thought to be only 13 years old. North Korea has never been led by a woman, and she has not been formally designated as heir. Her youth would also leave her vulnerable in any power struggle.All of this uncertainty helps explain why rumours about Kim's health attract so much attention.The second reason is that the rumours are not entirely implausible.Kim is overweight and a heavy smoker. South Korea's National Intelligence Service has repeatedly warned that his lifestyle puts him at higher risk of cardiovascular disease. Heart problems and strokes also run in the Kim family.If anything were to happen to Kim, the stakes are high for neighbouring countries and the wider international community. Any sudden leadership crisis raises difficult questions about control of North Korea's nuclear weapons and the prospect of political instability.Would a power struggle tempt hardliners to act aggressively? Could unrest trigger a refugee crisis along the Chinese border? These are questions that concern not only Beijing and Seoul but also Washington, which maintains around 28,000 troops in South Korea.Intelligence agencies watch Kim Jong Un closely so they are prepared for any news.Because North Korea remains an information black hole, it is also an easy target for false reports. Only a tiny circle has regular access to its leader. Even intelligence agencies struggle to obtain reliable information, and much of what emerges is heavily caveated as unverified or highly likely rather than confirmed fact.The regime itself is also suspected of deliberately encouraging confusion, leaking misleading information to obscure what is really happening inside the country.So it is hard to believe that Wanjun Xie had somehow stumbled across such significant news, when it had eluded those whose job it is to stay across it. He may simply have been seeking attention. Or he may have wanted to embarrass Beijing by highlighting its ties to Pyongyang, although those are well-established for the world to see.Whatever his motive, Xie is far from the first person to exploit the uncertainty surrounding North Korea's leadership.

schema.headline: Kim Jong Un: Why do rumours about his death keep coming back?

title: Japan's MMX mission set to grab a piece of Mars's moon Phobos
description: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moonFigure caption, Watch: Spacecraft heading to Mars' moon Phobos lifts off from JapanByRebecca Mo
body: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moonFigure caption, Watch: Spacecraft heading to Mars' moon Phobos lifts off from JapanByRebecca MorelleAlison Francis and Kevin ChurchBBC News Science  A spacecraft has launched from Japan headed for Mars' moon Phobos, where it will attempt to grab some moondust and bring it back to Earth.If it is successful, this will become the first time a sample has been returned from Mars or its moons to be analysed in laboratories here on Earth. The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027.It is hoped that the Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which is led by the Japanese Space Agency, will solve the mystery of how Mars's moons formed.Prof Sara Russell, from the Natural History Museum, who is the MMX mission's deputy for sample analysis, said: "There hasn't yet been a successful mission to go to Phobos and bring a bit back to Earth. "I think this is an incredibly ambitious and fun mission," she said.There are only three moons in the inner Solar System: our own Moon, and two around Mars, which are called Phobos and Deimos.Both of these are tiny - Phobos is about 20km (12 miles) across and Deimos is about 10km (six miles) across. They are also irregularly shaped, looking a bit like space potatoes.The MMX spacecraft will study Deimos as it arrives in the Mars neighbourhood, and then will focus on Phobos.It plans to set down a small rover to explore the terrain, though this will be no easy feat.Sara Russell says no one has ever landed a rover on such a small moon."The moon itself doesn't have very much of its own gravity," she explained."But it's next to an enormous planet that's got a much higher gravity,  and that makes it much harder to get a rover onto the surface."Image source, NASAImage caption, Mars got its moons about 4.5bn years ago - but no one knows how they formedThe rover will scout out a landing site so that the MMX spacecraft itself can later touch down on Phobos.Once on the surface, it will deploy a robotic arm and two samplers to grab some moon dust.This material will be packed into a small capsule that will return to Earth in 2031, landing in the Woomera desert of South Australia.The amount of material that will come back is tiny - just 10g."It's a very small [amount] actually," said Dr Chrysa Avdellidou, from Leicester University, who is working with the Japanese mission.   "However we can do several studies even on individual grains… You don't need to have kilos back from a surface in order to do science.  So it's worth every gram," she said.Image source, JAXAImage caption, The spacecraft will collect 10g of moon dust from the surface of PhobosScientists believe the sample will finally shed light on the puzzle of where Mars's moons came from.There are two competing ideas.Either a space rock smashed into Mars early in its history, and Phobos and Deimos were created from the debris.Or the moons are two wandering asteroids from the outer Solar System, which were grabbed by the Red Planet's gravity."When we get the sample back, we'll be able to look in detail at its chemistry and its mineral composition - and the two hypotheses will produce very distinct results," said Sara Russell."It should be pretty much immediately obvious.. whether it's the product of this dramatic impact or whether it's a captured asteroid. So we'll find that out really quickly."The team is also hoping there might be an extra bonus coming back to their labs."One of the really exciting things is that Phobos is so close to the Mars surface that whenever there's an impact into the Mars surface, little grains might actually become implanted into Phobos itself," said Russell."And that means that the sample we get back may actually contain grains of Mars as well. So it can give us really direct information about the composition and history of Mars."Image source, Kevin Church/BBC NewsImage caption, Martian meteorites are rare - this one is on display at the Natural History Museum  Bringing material from Mars back to Earth has long been an ambition of space scientists.The Nasa Perseverance rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, has been carefully collecting samples on Mars and storing them in canisters.But a second Nasa/ESA mission, called Mars Sample Return, that would have picked up and returned these canisters, has been effectively cancelled, after its funding was halted by the US Congress.China is planning its own sampling mission to Mars, set to launch in 2028. It will attempt to return Martian material to Earth in 2031.We do already have some fragments of the Red Planet here on Earth in the form of Martian meteorites.These are pieces of Mars that were blasted off the surface by asteroid strikes, and ended up being hurled towards the Earth.Martian meteorites are extremely rare, but like all space rocks that fall to our planet, they become contaminated as soon as they get here, mixing with the air, dust, soil and water.Scientists are so desperate to get their gloved hands on a direct sample from Mars and its moons because it would be pristine.

schema.headline: Japan's MMX mission set to grab a piece of Mars's moon Phobos

title: Vance tells Republicans to 'stop whining' about Ohio attack ad against Democrat Amy Acton
description: US Vice-President JD Vance has urged fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about a controversial attack ad that featured a Democratic candidate's estra
body: US Vice-President JD Vance has urged fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about a controversial attack ad that featured a Democratic candidate's estranged mother calling her a liar. While campaigning in Ohio for Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor, Vance said he was "a little bit disgusted" by criticism from members of his own party. In the ad, Donna Arthur, the mother of Democratic candidate Amy Acton, said her daughter "lied her entire life". It does not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child.The Ramaswamy campaign have claimed credit for the ad, and have paid millions to have it advertised around the state. Acton's brother is among those who have condemned the ad, saying turning alleged sexual assault into "a political talking point" was a "despicable low". Acton and her brother were removed from their mother's custody when her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged in 1978. That is when she last spoke to her mother, Acton said in an interview with The Vindicator, an Ohio news outlet. The Arthurs fled Ohio and Cledith Arthur was never prosecuted on the rape charge. He died in 2004.When the ad featuring Donna Arthur was initially released to social media on Monday evening, it did not say who the video was paid for or authorised by. Ramaswamy confirmed on Tuesday that it came from his campaign, and he later pledged to spend $4m (£2.9m) to further air it.The move has drawn a bipartisan backlash.Former South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley, who ran against Ramaswamy for the Republican nomination for president in 2024, said "he's a bad guy. It's a shame he continues to get away with it". Vance, when asked by BBC News if he thought the ad was appropriate, answered: "It's not really my concern.""What is my concern is who's going to govern the next generation of American government."He also said he was "a little bit disgusted" by members of his own party who "are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America". Vance, a former Ohio senator, later defended the ad at a rally for Ramaswamy, saying: "Now the media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is, and calls Amy Acton a liar."When asked about Ramaswamy's ad on Wednesday, Trump said: "I know nothing about it. I heard the mother went very rogue on the daughter."He added: "It's a very unusual situation to have a mother hate a daughter that much. But I dont think that has anything to do with Vivek."Acton's team released its own campaign ad on Tuesday, a video featuring her brother, Philip Stearns, recounting childhood abuse and saying "Amy always got the worst of it"."Shame on Vivek," he says in the 30-second clip. "It's the contempt he has for Amy. It's the contempt he has for Ohio."Other Republicans, including ones running for statewide office, have now criticised the ad.Ohio Senator John Husted, who is up for re-election, told the Associated Press: "I would not have run that ad."Ohio Secretary of Frank LaRose, who is running to be state auditor, was another Republican coming out against the ad. "I will say that, you know, candidates will answer for their own ads, that, you know, I probably wouldn't run an ad like that, but every candidate gets to make their own decision," he told WSYX-TV, external in the city of Columbus.Political attack ads are not a new feature of US politics, but David Lublin, a professor from American University's School of Public Affairs, told the BBC that "they have become more intense, and the boundaries have stretched in terms of what one attacks about". Lublin said it was not new for relatives to be used against a political opponent, mentioning family members who testified against Robert F Kennedy Jr before he was confirmed as health secretary. "But this is of a different order," he said. "They're estranged not over policy but over a rape allegation." Lublin believes President Donald Trump's rhetoric and campaigns have helped act as a catalyst for the coarsening of American political discourse - mentioning the time Trump mocked a reporter in Ohio who had a disability."We live in an age where certainly many candidates can appear mean and even inappropriate at times," Lublin said, adding: "The key purpose of attack ads isn't necessarily to convert the followers of your opponent, but more to depress their turnout."He expects the Ramaswamy attack ad to backfire, saying it could be an indication that his campaign is desperate to swing momentum in his favour in the increasingly competitive race for Ohio governor - even though a Democrat has not been elected governor there in over two decades.Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan website that rates and tracks US elections, has moved the Ohio governor's race from "leans Republican" to "toss up", meaning neither candidate has a clear advantage.

schema.headline: Vance tells Republicans to 'stop whining' about Ohio attack ad against Democrat Amy Acton

title: Helen Haines: 'Targeted' attack on much-loved Australian MP leaves Wangaratta heartbroken
description: Wangaratta has been thrust into an unwelcome spotlight this week. Residents in this rural Victorian town are used to catering to tourists passing thro
body: Wangaratta has been thrust into an unwelcome spotlight this week. Residents in this rural Victorian town are used to catering to tourists passing through on their way to regional wineries, or music lovers visiting its annual jazz and blues festival.Instead, locals are fielding endless questions about their MP - and having to explain to strangers what it all means for the town's nearly 30,000 people.They are clearly in shock about what police say was a targeted and deliberate attack on Helen Haines on Monday afternoon, when she was struck by a car just outside her office."People are simply dumbfounded and finding it very hard to fathom the scale of this tragedy," Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who represents King Charles, said at a press conference on Wednesday.The independent federal MP had to have both legs amputated after she was airlifted to Melbourne. But the "two most important parts of Helen", her heart and her mind, were in "good shape", her husband Phil Haines said.The MP isn't a divisive figure, locals tell the BBC, and no one can understand why she was allegedly targeted."Everyone knows Helen," says Jane Hill, who owns a giftware shop a few hundred metres down the town's main street from where Haines was hit."She is a such a good person in our community. She'd go to everything - celebrations, funerals, she's one of those genuinely kind people - and so are her family."Local man Brendan Nugent, whose father has been good friends with Haines for decades, faces at least three charges over the alleged attack including intentionally causing harm and appeared in court on Wednesday. Police say they are considering further charges, including attempted murder.First elected to parliament in 2019, Haines is best known for her years-long efforts to establish a national anti-corruption commission.She was spurred on by a series of major political scandals which, in her words, saw "public money spent for political gain", disproportionate spending on "shiny infrastructure projects" in marginal seats and decisions benefitting big donors over ordinary people.The commission finally opened in 2023 under Anthony Albanese's Labor government.Haines has also helped to secure funds for housebuilding, railway improvements and health infrastructure in her region, which she argues has long been sidelined by policies favouring cities.On a spring afternoon in Wangaratta, nobody seemed to have a bad word to say about the former nurse and midwife turned politician.Local Mayor Irene Grant described her as "warm", "cheerful" and "committed", and pointed to her record on climate action and Indigenous rights.In a police update on Wednesday, Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush said she'd given "wonderful support" to local police when two officers were shot dead in the nearby town of Porepunkah last year.Bystanders who came to Haines' aid recalled how she thanked them even as she lay severely injured."It was incredible," Jacklyn Black told Nine Network's Today show. "We were having conversations, she was telling me about her grandkids.""To be in that situation and be as calm as she could be in the moment, but also thankful to the aid that the community had given her... I could [not] speak any more highly of her in a moment like that," Cody Lepoidevin added."She just thanked everyone."There's a large print-out of Helen Haines plastered onto the window of her office - anyone delivering flowers for her gets a big smile back as they look up and walk away.Across the road on Tuesday, a man waved an Australian flag. On his T-shirt were the words "Wangaratta - this is not us!!"It's clear that many feel that way in this friendly community where people look out for each other.Next door to Haines' office is RickyChops barbershop, owned by Ricky Jefferies. When he heard the chaos unfolding outside, he rushed to help, pinning down the suspect."I just leant over him and once he was on the ground and he was no longer a threat, I just stood with him, and I told him that he can't leave," he explained after the incident."I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I just was a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish sort of way."Some clearly disagree with Ricky. By Tuesday afternoon, he too had received a bouquet of flowers tied to his shop's door, and a small balloon with the words "thank you".Down the road at the Holy Trinity Anglican Cathedral, a vigil was held, attended by a couple of hundred people lining up to light a candle for Haines.Some hugged the clergy, while others wore campaign T-shirts carrying the words "Team Helen Haines".Her husband Phil said he had received "thousands upon thousands" of messages of love and support."I can only say how much of a difference that makes to all of us," he said. "Helen's road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter.""Whether you vote for her or not, she seems to have the community at heart so that's all you can really ask for; a politician that represents your community," said Austin Longfield who lives in nearby Albury."It's just something that you wouldn't expect in our community," he added. "You see it in other countries and it's just something that I didn't comprehend could happen here."With additional reporting by Simon Atkinson

schema.headline: Helen Haines: 'Targeted' attack on much-loved Australian MP leaves Wangaratta heartbroken

title: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots for political gain
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Protesters rallied in Lille along with other cities across the countryByPatrick JacksonMarco Silva an
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Protesters rallied in Lille along with other cities across the countryByPatrick JacksonMarco Silva and Thomas CopelandBBC Verify French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the  riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes.Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests.Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic".It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month.Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots.Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice.Video of running battles between masked rioters and police, as well as property being destroyed and stores being looted, spread across social media.   The government admitted the police had "lost control" during the violence, which came after weeks of protests by students over conditions in high schools. Macron vowed afterwards that the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups", which he blamed for much of the trouble.Speaking in the Qatari capital Doha, the French president said: "For me, there is no visible foreign interference in the events that took place. On the other hand, there was foreign manipulation of information afterwards, yes, and that gave rise to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders... "We had people claiming that we had been invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false."On Tuesday, Netanyahu said in an interview for Israel's i24 channel, external that France, which has Western Europe's largest Muslim minority, had been hit by an "invasion of extremist Islam".He said he had told Macron after the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023: "If we do not eliminate them here, you will have them in Paris." "That is exactly what is happening," he added.Also on Tuesday, Trump blamed the riots on mass immigration to France. "When I look at France, when you look at Italy, when you look at all the turmoil and the hatred, that's not about school," he said. "That's about people coming into the countries that hate the country.""Close your borders and take control before it is too late!" he said in remarks directed at Macron.According to a report in the UK's Financial Times newspaper, external, EU regulators are examining possible foreign online interference and disinformation campaigns around the French riots and similar recent outbursts of unrest in EU states.It quotes unnamed security officials as saying that pro-Russian and far-right social media accounts linked to previous disinformation campaigns have spread violent videos in an attempt to sow more chaos.Iran and Algeria are also suspected of being behind some of the messaging, the paper adds.David Colon, a researcher at France's Sciences Po university who specialises in disinformation, was quoted as saying that "pro-Kremlin influencers" linked to the Russian campaign Storm-1516 had "amplified the events and spread a number of false narratives".France is one of Ukraine's most vociferous military supporters in its ongoing war with Russia, while Algeria is a former French colony with bitter memories of its war to achieve independence in 1962, and French relations with Iran have been strained by its war with the US and Israel this year.         BBC Verify has reviewed more than 15 examples of fake news videos on social media which researchers at the US-based dTeam say are the work of a Russian disinformation operation known as Matryoshka.The videos feature near-identical branding to real news outlets in France, including Le Monde, Euronews and France 24.The individual impact and reach of videos made by Matryoshka appear to be limited, but experts have said the focus on amplifying unrest is consistent with known Russian disinformation tactics.Separately, BBC Verify has traced one of the most viral AI-generated images circulating on social media, which supposedly shows an elderly couple being robbed and left in their underwear in Paris, to an obscure website.The director of Infos-Israel.News, Sabrina Hania, told the BBC her team had created the image - which was published on 17 October - using ChatGPT without using a reference image.It was posted shortly after a television journalist reported on the alleged incident, citing "police information". The claim remains unconfirmed, with French media reporting that prosecutors have no information supporting it having happened.While the original image was labelled as "Made with AI" on X and "AI content" on Instagram, it was later shared on X without any disclaimer in a post which attracted more than six million views.Hania said she regretted that the image had been taken out of context and had misled so many people, blaming those who reshared it without identifying it as AI-generated.

schema.headline: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots for political gain

title: Elon Musk confirms he is considering merging Tesla and SpaceX
description: Image source, Courtesy/XImage caption, Elon Musk is chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla ByKali HaysTechnology reporterUpdated 21 October 2026Elon
body: Image source, Courtesy/XImage caption, Elon Musk is chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla ByKali HaysTechnology reporterUpdated 21 October 2026Elon Musk has said he is actively considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two biggest companies.  "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts to discuss SpaceX's latest results on Tuesday.While Musk noted it could not be assumed a merger will go ahead, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies had been formed to examine the move."The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," he said. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.SpaceX builds space rockets as well as Starlink internet satellites and provides a secured satellite network for governments, including the US, through its Starshield business.    That part of the business is currently facing scrutiny over claims Ukraine's access to the network has been limited, leaving it vulnerable to deadly strikes by Russia.US President Donald Trump has denied either he or Musk ordered the slowdown. Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions.Starlink's total revenue rose to $5.2bn in the three months to 30 September from $3bn in the same period last year. It is dwarfed by SpaceX's expansion into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, such as Anthropic and Google.The business generated revenues of $7.5bn over the three months, up from $813m last year.'Tap dancing through a minefield'Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger. He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of both Tesla and SpaceX.Even commenting on the possibility of combining the two companies, Musk compared it to "tap dancing through a minefield".A merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, he added. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve a combination, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve".Shareholders have supported Musk's desires before. Last year, a majority of investors in Tesla approved a compensation package for Musk valued at around $1tn.While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics. SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its market debut in June.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Elon Musk and Donald Trump have denied limiting Ukraine's access to SpaceX's Starshield networkSpaceX, as a whole is not profitable, despite revenue jumping to $27bn from $13.7bn over the first nine months of the year.Over that same period it lost $1.1bn although it did report a $4.4bn profit for the most recent three months.Following Musk's comments, SpaceX's share price rose 8% in after-hours trading. Shares in Tesla, which reports its own quarterly results on Wednesday, rose by 2% Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X, the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned.The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together.Musk said on Tuesday a full merger between the two companies would make sense for the work each is doing around chips, artificial intelligence and software.
